blocks.text: Benzene does undergo addition under forcing conditions. Hydrogenation adds hydrogen to the carbons of the ring; complete hydrogenation gives cyclohexane, a useful solvent and a starting material for other chemicals: C6H6 + 3H2 -> C6H12.

blocks.alt: Benzene + 3H2 gives cyclohexane, a ring of six CH2 groups. Methylbenzene + 3H2 gives methylcyclohexane, a ring of one CH carrying CH3 and five CH2 groups.
blocks.caption: Hydrogenation of benzene and methylbenzene (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 70).

blocks.text: These reactions destroy the delocalisation of the benzene ring, because the pi electrons are used to form bonds to the new hydrogen atoms. The reactions are exothermic overall, because the new C-H bonds are strong, but they have a high activation barrier. They use the same finely divided nickel catalyst as the hydrogenation of alkenes, at similar temperatures (around 150 C) but at higher pressure.
Chlorine and bromine add in the same way. Without a catalyst, UV light and heat are enough for complete addition: C6H6 + 3Cl2 -> C6H6Cl6 (1,2,3,4,5,6-hexachlorocyclohexane).

blocks.alt: Benzene + 3Cl2, with UV, heat over the arrow, gives hexachlorocyclohexane: a six-membered ring of single bonds with one H and one Cl on every carbon.
blocks.caption: Complete chlorination of benzene (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 71).
